name: Citizenship by Descent (Jus Sanguinis)

requirements.blocker_text: This requires at least one parent being a Swiss citizen at the time of your birth (father or mother, in or out of wedlock, with paternity established for out-of-wedlock cases). Citizenship is attributed automatically at birth, whether in Switzerland or abroad.

If born abroad and also holding another nationality, this requires notifying a Swiss authority (abroad or in Switzerland) of the birth, OR declaring in writing the wish to retain Swiss citizenship, before turning 25 — failure to do so results in AUTOMATIC LOSS of Swiss citizenship at that age (Art. 7 SCA). Children of a person who lost citizenship under this rule likewise lose it.
requirements.fix_path: Complete the registration or declaration with a Swiss authority before age 25.

evidence_required.document: Birth certificate and evidence of the parent's Swiss citizenship at time of birth
Registration/declaration with a Swiss authority before age 25 (for those born abroad with dual nationality)

outcome.duration_length: indefinite (subject to the age-25 loss provision for those born abroad)

sources.title: Swiss Citizenship Act (SCA), Art. 1-7 - State Secretariat for Migration

notes: STALE-DATA CORRECTION confirmed during research: the loss-of-citizenship deadline for those born abroad with dual nationality is AGE 25, not age 22 as some tier-3 sites still claim — a real and specific figure error worth catching. This age-25 rule is genuinely unusual among the ancestry routes in this dataset — most other countries' descent routes (France, Japan, Australia) attribute citizenship at birth with no subsequent loss condition; Switzerland's automatic-loss-if-not-registered mechanic is a real structural outlier, closer in spirit to Japan's separate age-based choice-of-nationality rule (though Japan's is a CHOICE between nationalities, while Switzerland's is a registration/notification requirement to simply RETAIN citizenship already held). Genuine live legal debate exists in Switzerland about this rule's fairness given how common dual nationality has become through international marriage — no confirmed change had taken effect as of this verification; encoded as current law, not anticipated reform.
